The curved line PQR is the velocity–time graph for a car starting from rest.
R

5

What is the average acceleration of the car over the first 5 s?
A
the area below the curve PQ
B
the area of the triangle PQS
C
the gradient of the straight line PQ
D
the gradient of the tangent at Q

hints: Notice P is at the origin with $v=0$ and Q is at $time = 5 \text{ s}$ - average acceleration depends only on these two end points, not the curve between them.
Recall that for a velocity-time graph, gradient means acceleration and area means displacement, so check units of $\text{m s}^{-2}$ versus $\text{m}$.
Compare the straight dashed chord PQ with the tangent at Q - one gives $\Delta v / 5$ for the whole interval and the other gives the slope at one instant.
walkthrough: Identify the interval: P is $t = 0$, $v = 0$ since the car starts from rest, and Q is $t = 5 \text{ s}$ with velocity equal to QS.
State the rule for average acceleration: $a_{avg} = \Delta v / \Delta t = (v_Q - v_P)/(5 - 0)$.
On a velocity-time graph, $\Delta v / \Delta t$ is rise over run, which is the gradient of the straight line joining the two end points.
The straight dashed line PQ joins exactly those end points, so its gradient is $v_Q / 5$, which equals the average acceleration.
Areas under PQ or triangle PQS have units of velocity $\times$ time and give displacement, while the tangent at Q gives instantaneous acceleration at $5 \text{ s}$ only.
Therefore the average over the first $5 \text{ s}$ is the gradient of the straight line PQ. This is option C

A.explanation: Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement in $\text{m}$, not acceleration in $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: Triangle PQS approximates displacement but its area is larger than the true area under curve PQ, and area is not acceleration.

C.explanation: The chord PQ joins $v=0$ at $t=0$ to $v$ at $t=5 \text{ s}$, so its gradient equals $\Delta v / \Delta t$, the average acceleration.

D.explanation: The gradient of the tangent at Q gives the instantaneous acceleration at $t = 5 \text{ s}$, not the average over $0$ to $5 \text{ s}$.
